elements.text: Pilot's decision to take off from a remote, mountainous landing site in dark, windy, IMC conditions
Organizational culture prioritizing mission execution over aviation safety
Pilot's fatigue
Pilot's self-induced pressure to conduct the flight
Pilot's situational stress
Lack of a requirement for risk assessment during the mission
Inadequate pilot staffing
Lack of an effective fatigue management program for pilots
Inadequate procedures and equipment for communication between airborne and ground personnel
Helicopter was properly certificated and maintained
No evidence of preimpact structural, engine, or system failures
No evidence of preexisting medical or toxicological conditions affecting pilot performance
Seats and restraint systems functioned as designed but were exceeded by crash forces
Adverse weather and terrain hindered timely rescue, contributing to pilot's death from exposure
Pilot failed to mitigate risks by bringing survival gear or ensuring NVGs were available
Pilot exhibited poor decision-making by choosing to take off at night and attempt VFR in adverse weather
Pilot's fatigue, pressure, and stress distracted him from evaluating alternatives
Management actions emphasized accepting all missions without adequate regard for conditions, inconsistent with safety culture
Lack of structured, task-specific risk assessment programs
Flight and duty time policies did not ensure minimum contiguous rest periods
Staffing level was insufficient to allow 24/7 operations without creating unacceptable fatigue risk
Personnel did not regularly follow SAR plan or communicate directly with SAR commanders
Pilot lacked instrument rating, experience, and training for inadvertent IMC encounters
406-MHz ELT signals helped locate wreckage and survivor
Use of flight-tracking systems could shorten search times
